---
title: "Week 7: Data Visualization (Grammar of Graphics, Basic Geoms, Facets, Positions & Themes)"
output: html_notebook
---

```{r}
#Last week we learned to work with real survey data: selecting rows and columns, asking TRUE/FALSE questions,
##changing values and handling missing answers (NA).

#Today we turn data into PICTURES. A good plot shows in seconds what a table of 2,615 numbers can't:
##how answers are distributed, how two variables are related, and how groups differ.
##Today's plan:
##(1) Prepare the data (just like last week)
##(2) The grammar of graphics: the three ingredients of every ggplot
##(3) Plotting ONE variable: histograms and bar charts
##(4) Plotting TWO (or three) variables: boxplots and scatterplots
##(5) Comparing groups with facets
##(6) Positions: stacked, side-by-side and jittered
##(7) Making it look good: titles, themes, and saving your plot
```

# Preparing the Data

```{r}
#ggplot2 is the plotting package we use. You already installed it in our packages week (remember qplot()?),
##so we only need to load it -- at the start of EVERY session, together with haven:
library(ggplot2)
library(haven)

#Load the TGSS data, exactly like last week:
tgss <- read_sav("TGSS2024.sav")

#Keep only the variables we need today:
##age, gender, happy ("How happy do you feel?" 1-5), trustpeople ("How much do you trust people?" 0-10),
##height (in cm) and weight (in kg)
tg <- tgss[, c("id", "age", "gender", "happy", "trustpeople", "height", "weight")]

#The same two clean-up steps as last week:
tg <- as.data.frame(tg)   #tibble -> classic data frame
tg <- zap_labels(tg)      #remove the SPSS labels -> plain numbers

str(tg)
```

```{r}
#Last week we said: "We'll bring labels back when we need them for plots." That time is now!
##Why? ggplot looks at the TYPE of a variable to decide how to draw it:
##numbers are treated as continuous (a smooth scale), factors are treated as categories (separate groups).
##gender and happy are categories, so we turn them into factors with readable labels (Week 4!).

#factor(variable, levels = the codes in the data, labels = what the codes mean -- in the same order, from the codebook)
tg$gender_f <- factor(tg$gender, levels = c(1, 2), labels = c("Male", "Female"))

tg$happy_f <- factor(tg$happy, levels = c(1, 2, 3, 4, 5),
                     labels = c("Extremely unhappy", "Unhappy", "Neither", "Happy", "Extremely happy"))

#Check: table() shows the labels instead of the numbers now
table(tg$gender_f)
table(tg$happy_f, useNA = "ifany")   #people who didn't answer stay NA

#We keep the original numeric columns too -- the _f ("factor") versions are new columns.
```

# The Grammar of Graphics

```{r}
#Every ggplot is built from the same three ingredients -- this is the "grammar of graphics":
##(1) DATA:       which data frame?                                    -> ggplot(data = tg)
##(2) AESTHETICS: which variable goes where (x-axis, y-axis, color)?   -> aes(x = age)
##(3) GEOM:       which shape draws the data (bars, points, boxes)?    -> geom_histogram()
##The pieces are joined with a + sign, like building a plot layer by layer.

#Let's build one step by step and look at the result after each step:

#Step 1 -- only the data: R prepares an empty canvas
ggplot(data = tg)
```

```{r}
#Step 2 -- add the aesthetics: now ggplot knows that age goes on the x-axis, so it draws the axis
ggplot(data = tg, aes(x = age))
```

```{r}
#Step 3 -- add a geom: now the data is actually drawn, as a histogram
ggplot(data = tg, aes(x = age)) +
  geom_histogram()

#WATCH OUT: the + must be at the END of a line, never at the start of the next one.
##If a line starts with +, R thinks the plot was already finished on the line before.
```

# Plotting ONE Variable: Distributions

```{r}
#A HISTOGRAM shows the distribution of a NUMERIC variable: how many people fall into each range of values.
##The message "stat_bin() using bins = 30" means ggplot chose the width of the bars for us.
##We can choose it ourselves with binwidth -- here, each bar covers 5 years of age:
ggplot(data = tg, aes(x = age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5)

#Remember qplot(rolls, binwidth = 1) from our dice weeks? qplot() was a quick shortcut for ggplot().
##It is now outdated, so from today on we write the full ggplot() version.
```

```{r}
#Changing the color of the bars: fill = the inside color, color = the border color
ggplot(data = tg, aes(x = age)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "steelblue", color = "white")

#Notice: fill and color are written INSIDE geom_histogram(), not inside aes().
##That means "make ALL bars this color". (Inside aes() means something else -- we'll see it in a minute.)
```

```{r}
#A BAR CHART shows the distribution of a CATEGORICAL variable (a factor): how many people are in each category.
ggplot(data = tg, aes(x = happy_f)) +
  geom_bar()

#If some people didn't answer the question, you will see a gray "NA" bar on the right.
```

```{r}
#To leave out the people who didn't answer, use logical subsetting from last week:
##!is.na(...) means "NOT missing" -> keep only the rows where happy_f has an answer
tg_happy <- tg[!is.na(tg$happy_f), ]

ggplot(data = tg_happy, aes(x = happy_f)) +
  geom_bar(fill = "darkorange")

#Histogram or bar chart? Ask yourself what kind of variable you have:
##numeric (age, height...)          -> geom_histogram()
##categorical / factor (happy_f...) -> geom_bar()
```

# Plotting TWO Variables: Relationships

```{r}
#Psychology question: do happier people trust others more?
##A BOXPLOT compares a NUMERIC variable (trustpeople) across the groups of a CATEGORICAL variable (happy_f).
##So now we need two aesthetics: x = the groups, y = the numeric variable.
ggplot(data = tg_happy, aes(x = happy_f, y = trustpeople)) +
  geom_boxplot()

#How to read a boxplot:
##the thick line in the middle = the median (half of the people are above it, half below)
##the box = the middle 50% of the people
##the lines (whiskers) = the rest of the typical range; single dots = unusual values (outliers)

#You may see a warning like "Removed ... rows containing non-finite values":
##those are people with NA on trustpeople. ggplot can't draw a missing value, so it skips them and tells you.
```

```{r}
#A SCATTERPLOT shows the relationship between TWO NUMERIC variables: one point per person.
ggplot(data = tg, aes(x = height, y = weight)) +
  geom_point()

#Taller people tend to be heavier -- the cloud of points goes up from left to right.
##You will get a "Removed ... rows" warning again: height and weight were not asked to everyone, so many people have NA.
##ggplot simply leaves them out of the plot.
```

```{r}
#Adding a THIRD variable with color: put color INSIDE aes() and give it a variable.
##Inside aes() means "color the points ACCORDING TO this variable" -- ggplot picks the colors and adds a legend.
ggplot(data = tg, aes(x = height, y = weight, color = gender_f)) +
  geom_point()

#Compare with the histogram above:
##geom_histogram(fill = "steelblue")   -> OUTSIDE aes(): one fixed color for everything
##aes(color = gender_f)                -> INSIDE aes(): the color shows the values of a variable
```

```{r}
#Too many points on top of each other? alpha makes them see-through (0 = invisible, 1 = solid).
##Dark areas now show where many people are.
ggplot(data = tg, aes(x = height, y = weight, color = gender_f)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4)
```

# Comparing Groups: Facets

```{r}
#Color is one way to compare groups. Another way is FACETS: one small plot per group, side by side.
##facet_wrap(~ variable) splits the plot by the categories of that variable. Read the ~ as "split by".
ggplot(data = tg, aes(x = height, y = weight)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  facet_wrap(~ gender_f)

#Same data as the colored scatterplot above -- but now men and women each get their own panel.
##Facets are especially useful when colors would overlap too much.
```

```{r}
#Facets work with any geom. Psychology question: do men and women answer the happiness question differently?
ggplot(data = tg_happy, aes(x = happy_f)) +
  geom_bar() +
  facet_wrap(~ gender_f, ncol = 1)

#ncol = 1 puts the panels on top of each other (1 column), so the long category names have enough space.
```

# Positions: Stacked, Side by Side, Jittered

```{r}
#Another way to compare two CATEGORICAL variables in one bar chart: fill the bars with a second variable.
##fill = gender_f goes INSIDE aes(), because the color shows the values of a variable.
ggplot(data = tg_happy, aes(x = happy_f, fill = gender_f)) +
  geom_bar()

#By default, the bars are STACKED on top of each other: position = "stack".
```

```{r}
#position = "dodge" puts the bars SIDE BY SIDE -- easier to compare men and women in each category:
ggplot(data = tg_happy, aes(x = happy_f, fill = gender_f)) +
  geom_bar(position = "dodge")
```

```{r}
#position = "fill" stretches every bar to the same height (1 = 100%), so you compare PROPORTIONS instead of counts:
##"Among the extremely happy, what share are women?" -- useful when the groups have very different sizes.
ggplot(data = tg_happy, aes(x = happy_f, fill = gender_f)) +
  geom_bar(position = "fill") +
  labs(y = "proportion")   #the y-axis now shows proportions, not counts, so we rename it
```

```{r}
#Positions also solve a common problem with survey scales. Let's make a scatterplot of happy (1-5) and trustpeople (0-10):
ggplot(data = tg, aes(x = happy, y = trustpeople)) +
  geom_point()

#Only a grid of dots! Answers can only be whole numbers, so hundreds of people sit on exactly the same spot.
##You can't see where most people are.
```

```{r}
#geom_jitter() moves every point a tiny random distance, so the hidden points become visible.
##width and height control how far the points may move -- keep them small (less than half a step on the scale).
ggplot(data = tg, aes(x = happy, y = trustpeople)) +
  geom_jitter(width = 0.2, height = 0.2, alpha = 0.3)

#Now the dark clouds show where most respondents are. Jitter changes only the PICTURE -- the data itself stays the same.
```

# Making It Look Good: Titles, Themes and Saving

```{r}
#A plot for a report or a thesis needs clear labels. labs() changes the title and the axis/legend names:
ggplot(data = tg, aes(x = height, y = weight, color = gender_f)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(title = "Height and weight of TGSS 2024 respondents",
       x = "Height (cm)",
       y = "Weight (kg)",
       color = "Gender")
```

```{r}
#A THEME changes the overall look of the plot (background, grid lines, fonts) -- not the data.
##ggplot has several ready-made themes, each added with one more + line. Try a few:
ggplot(data = tg, aes(x = height, y = weight, color = gender_f)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  theme_minimal()   #also try: theme_classic(), theme_bw()
```

```{r}
#theme() lets you customize details yourself. Here: bigger text, and the legend at the bottom of the plot.
##Put it AFTER the ready-made theme, otherwise the ready-made theme overwrites your changes.
ggplot(data = tg, aes(x = height, y = weight, color = gender_f)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4) +
  labs(title = "Height and weight of TGSS 2024 respondents",
       x = "Height (cm)",
       y = "Weight (kg)",
       color = "Gender") +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(text = element_text(size = 14), legend.position = "bottom")
```

```{r}
#ggsave() saves the LAST plot you made as an image file in your working directory (check with getwd()).
##width and height are in inches; the file type comes from the ending of the file name (.png, .pdf, .jpg).
##bg = "white" gives the image a white background (some themes, like theme_minimal(), are otherwise see-through).
ggsave("height_weight.png", width = 6, height = 4, bg = "white")
```
